lead: Cooling keeps metal alive, lubrication keeps it moving, and supercharging makes a small engine breathe like a big one. This unit covers all three, plus scavenging in two-stroke engines. After it you can size a coolant pump, pick an oil grade, explain turbo lag and read a scavenging diagram.
about: The unit follows the heat and the friction. Chapter 4.1 asks why an engine must be cooled at all and compares air cooling with liquid cooling. Chapter 4.2 goes inside the liquid system: thermosyphon, forced circulation, pressure caps and coolants. Chapter 4.3 turns to friction and the oil circuits that fight it, and 4.4 covers what makes a good lubricant. Chapters 4.5 to 4.7 deal with boosting: why supercharge, how a turbocharger differs, then variable geometry and intercooling. Chapter 4.8 closes with scavenging, where a two-stroke uses a blower to sweep out burnt gas. Each chapter uses numbers from a running engine, so the formulas stay tied to a real machine.

chapters.idea: Only about a quarter of the fuel energy becomes brake power; the rest is heat that must leave the engine, and cooling is the path it takes.
chapters.depth: Cover the need for cooling: metal strength falls with temperature, lubricating oil breaks down above roughly 150 °C at the rings, and uneven cooling causes thermal stress and distortion. Explain the split of fuel energy into brake power, exhaust heat, coolant heat and friction. Then the two families: air cooling with fins, fin spacing, baffles and blower-assisted flow, used on motorcycles and small gensets; liquid cooling with jackets, radiator, pump, thermostat and fan, used on cars and tractors. Compare them on heat transfer, weight, cost, noise, warm-up and maintenance. Some syllabi call the liquid type 'indirect cooling'. Do not derive heat transfer coefficients.

figure.title: Where the fuel energy goes
figure.aria: Flow of heat from fuel energy through the coolant jacket and radiator to the air, with the pump and fan keeping circulation going.
figure.caption: The jacket box carries roughly a quarter of the fuel energy; the pump and fan only move that heat outward.

chapters.example: A genset engine burns 8 kg of diesel per hour. Calorific value is 42000 kJ/kg. Fuel power = 8 × 42000 / 3600 = 93.3 kW. Thirty percent goes to the coolant: Q = 0.30 × 93.3 = 28 kW. Allowed water rise is 6 K, and specific heat of water c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K. Coolant flow ṁ = Q / (c ΔT) = 28 / (4.18 × 6) = 1.12 kg/s, about 67 kg per minute.
chapters.trap: Students take 30 percent of brake power instead of fuel power. The coolant carries a share of the fuel energy, so start from fuel flow times calorific value, never from the kW on the nameplate.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for engine components and the four-stroke cycle; Unit 5 for heat balance.
chapters.leave: Detailed heat balance table to Unit 5; radiator and fin heat transfer theory is outside this unit.

chapters.idea: A liquid cooling system can circulate by density difference alone, by a pump, or under pressure, and the coolant itself decides the safe upper temperature.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this at full depth. Cover three arrangements. Thermosyphon: hot water is lighter, rises from the jacket to the radiator, cools, falls back; give the driving pressure head formula and its limits at low engine speed. Forced circulation: pump driven by the engine, thermostat, bypass, pressure cap, expansion tank. Pressure cooling: a spring cap raises the boiling point, allowing a higher coolant temperature and a smaller radiator; state the pressure-to-boiling-point relation and the risk of a hot cap. Coolants: water, hard water problems, ethylene glycol and propylene glycol, antifreeze concentration, corrosion inhibitors, and why 50 percent glycol is common. Keep derivations out; the loop diagram and the numbers matter.

figure.title: Thermosyphon loop
figure.aria: Closed loop in which hot water rises from the engine jacket to the radiator, cools, and falls back through the downcomer.
figure.caption: The loop has no pump; the pressure difference between the hot and cold columns drives the flow.

chapters.example: A thermosyphon system has 0.4 m between the jacket centre and the radiator centre. Water at 40 °C has density 995 kg/m³ and at 80 °C it is 977 kg/m³. Driving pressure = (ρ cold − ρ hot) g h = (995 − 977) × 9.81 × 0.4 = 70.6 Pa. This small head gives gentle flow, which is why the same engine needs a pump once speed and load rise.
chapters.trap: A pressure cap does not cool the engine. It raises the boiling point, so the coolant can run hotter without boiling; if the cap is faulty the engine boils at a lower temperature.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for why heat must leave and for the radiator layout.
chapters.leave: Pump cavitation and radiator core design to a heat transfer course; coolant chemistry to the property tables given in the exam.

chapters.idea: Friction eats a fixed share of indicated power, and the lubrication system exists to keep that share small by feeding clean oil at the right pressure to every sliding pair.
chapters.depth: Cover sources of friction: piston rings and skirt, bearings, valve train, and pumping losses, which are grouped with friction in a motoring test. Explain hydrodynamic lubrication in one paragraph with the idea of an oil wedge, and boundary and mixed lubrication at start-up. Then the systems: mist or petroil lubrication for two-strokes, splash, pressure feed, wet sump with strainer, pump, relief valve, filter and gallery, dry sump with scavenge pump and tank. Give mechanical efficiency = brake power / indicated power and friction power = indicated − brake. Keep the friction mean effective pressure formula as a definition only.

figure.title: Wet sump oil circuit
figure.aria: Oil path in a wet sump engine from the sump through strainer, pump, filter and main gallery to the bearings, then draining back to the sump.
figure.caption: The dashed return line closes the circuit; a relief valve beside the pump limits maximum pressure.

chapters.example: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine is motored at 3000 rpm with the fuel cut off and the dynamometer reads 24 N·m. Friction power = 2π N T / 60 = 2π × 3000 × 24 / 60 = 7540 W = 7.54 kW. On a firing test the indicated power is 30 kW. Brake power = 30 − 7.54 = 22.46 kW. Mechanical efficiency = 22.46 / 30 = 0.749, that is 74.9 percent.
chapters.trap: Mechanical efficiency is brake power divided by indicated power, not the other way round. Motoring torque also includes pumping loss, so it is friction plus pumping, not pure rubbing friction.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for bearings, rings and the crank train; Unit 5 for indicated, brake and friction power definitions.
chapters.leave: Detailed friction power measurement to Unit 5; hydrodynamic theory and bearing design to machine design.

chapters.idea: A lubricant is chosen by its viscosity behaviour, its stability and its additives, not by how thick it feels.
chapters.depth: Cover the property list with units: viscosity and its units, viscosity index, pour point, flash point, fire point, cloud point, carbon residue, acidity and neutralisation number, oxidation stability, oiliness, emulsification and foaming. Explain multigrade oils, why 10W-40 behaves as a 10 grade when cold and a 40 grade when hot, and what the W means. Then additives: viscosity index improvers, antioxidants, detergents and dispersants, anti-wear and extreme pressure agents, corrosion and rust inhibitors, pour point depressants, antifoam. Add oil consumption: causes such as ring blow-by, valve guides and volatility, and the common way of stating it as a fraction of fuel used.

figure.aria: Tree grouping lubricant properties into physical, chemical and additive families, with the property each one controls.
figure.caption: Additives are the small third branch; they change the base oil's behaviour but do not replace it.

chapters.example: A car covers 1000 km and its owner tops up 0.4 litre of engine oil. Fuel average is 15 km per litre. Fuel used = 1000 / 15 = 66.7 litre. Oil consumption as a fraction of fuel = 0.4 / 66.7 = 0.006, that is 0.6 percent. Racing and worn engines run nearer 2 percent; a good road engine stays well below 1 percent.
chapters.trap: A higher viscosity number is not automatically better. Too thick an oil starves narrow passages when cold and raises churning loss; the grade must match the ambient range and the engine design.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.3 for where the oil goes and what it must do there.
chapters.leave: Additive chemistry and refinery processes are outside this unit; oil pump sizing belongs with the lubrication circuit in 4.3.

chapters.idea: Supercharging pushes more air mass into the same swept volume, so more fuel can be burnt and more power comes out of a smaller engine.
chapters.depth: Cover objectives: more power for the same size, better power-to-weight, altitude compensation, and in some cases better specific fuel consumption. Give the density ratio idea: power roughly follows trapped air mass, which follows pressure ratio and charge temperature. Types: mechanically driven blowers, roots, vane and centrifugal, with the roots and centrifugal sketches. Explain why a supercharger is a net loss on the crank and how that limits boost. Effects of supercharging: higher peak pressure and temperature, greater knock tendency in SI engines, need for lower compression ratio or better fuel, higher thermal loading, and effect on exhaust and emissions. State the necessity and, clearly, the limitations.

figure.title: Mechanical supercharger path
figure.aria: Air passing from the filter through a belt-driven supercharger into the intake manifold at higher pressure and temperature, then into the engine.
figure.caption: The blower raises pressure to 1.6 bar but also heats the air to 340 K, so density rises less than pressure.

chapters.example: A 1.5 litre petrol engine gives 75 kW naturally aspirated at 1.0 bar and 300 K. A supercharger raises manifold pressure to 1.6 bar and charge temperature to 340 K. Density ratio = (1.6/1.0) × (300/340) = 1.41. Gross power = 75 × 1.41 = 106 kW. The blower absorbs 11 kW from the crank at this speed. Net power = 106 − 11 = 95 kW, a gain of 20 kW, about 27 percent.
chapters.trap: Quoting the gross figure. A crank-driven blower takes its drive power from the same shaft, so the honest answer is the net gain, and it is always smaller than the density ratio suggests.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for swept volume and volumetric efficiency; Unit 3 for knock, since boost raises knock tendency.
chapters.leave: Exhaust-driven boosting to 4.6; charge cooling to 4.7; engine modification detail to 4.7 and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A turbocharger runs the compressor on waste exhaust energy, which is free power but arrives late, and that delay is turbo lag.
chapters.depth: Cover the turbocharger layout: turbine wheel, shaft, compressor wheel, bearing housing, wastegate and its actuator. Methods of turbocharging: constant pressure and pulse turbocharging, single turbo, twin turbo in parallel or series, and briefly the difference from a crank-driven blower. Explain boost threshold and turbo lag as separate things: threshold is the speed below which boost cannot build, lag is the time to build it after a throttle step. Cover the matching idea: the compressor must sit in a good efficiency island at cruise and the turbine must not over-speed at rated power; wastegate control, and the anti-lag measures such as small turbine housing, twin-scroll and lightweight wheels. Mention the cooling down idling habit and oil coking in the bearing housing.

figure.aria: Timeline showing the throttle opened at zero, the turbine spooling up over the next second, and boost becoming full only after about 1.6 seconds.
figure.caption: The gap between the throttle bar and the full boost bar is the lag the driver feels.

chapters.example: A 2 litre four-stroke runs at 3000 rpm. Air flow = 2 × 10⁻³ m³ × (3000/2) per minute = 0.05 m³/s, and at 1.2 kg/m³ this is 0.06 kg/s. The compressor needs to raise the air by 62 K, with cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K. Compressor power = 0.06 × 1.005 × 62 = 3.74 kW. Exhaust flow is 0.062 kg/s, turbine cp = 1.15 kJ/kg·K, mechanical efficiency 0.65. Required turbine temperature drop = 3.74 / (0.062 × 1.15 × 0.65) = 80.7 K, so the exhaust must fall about 81 K across the turbine.
chapters.trap: Lag and boost threshold get mixed up. Threshold is a speed below which no boost is possible; lag is a time delay at a speed where boost is possible. Also, the turbo does not run on air; it runs on exhaust enthalpy.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.5 for pressure ratio and density ratio; Unit 5 for air flow measurement.
chapters.leave: Compressor and turbine maps in detail to a turbomachinery course; engine modification for boost to 4.7.

chapters.idea: Variable geometry fixes the low-speed boost problem by shrinking the turbine nozzle at low flow, and an intercooler recovers the density lost to compressor heating.
chapters.depth: Cover variable geometry turbochargers: moving vanes or a sliding nozzle ring change turbine inlet area, small area for fast spool at low speed, large area to avoid over-boost and high back pressure at high speed; the actuator and the reason VGT also helps emissions and exhaust braking. Compare with a wastegate and with a fixed turbine. Then intercooling: why charge heating costs density, air-to-air and air-to-water types, fitting before or after the throttle, and the effect on knock, volumetric efficiency, NOx and fuel consumption. Give the intercooler effectiveness idea. Include engine modifications for supercharging as a short list: lower compression ratio, stronger pistons and gaskets, larger injectors, better cooling and oil supply to the turbo.

figure.aria: Plot of boost pressure against engine speed comparing a fixed turbine, which is weak at low speed, with a variable geometry turbo that holds boost almost flat from 2000 rpm.
figure.caption: The variable geometry curve is already near 0.9 bar at 1200 rpm, where the fixed turbine has almost nothing.

chapters.example: Compressor inlet is 300 K at 1.0 bar and the pressure ratio is 1.6. Compressor efficiency is 0.70 and γ = 1.4, so (γ−1)/γ = 0.286. T2 = T1 [1 + (1.6^0.286 − 1)/0.70] = 300 [1 + (1.1438 − 1)/0.70] = 362 K. Without an intercooler, density ratio = 1.6 × 300/362 = 1.33. An intercooler cools the charge to 315 K, giving density ratio = 1.6 × 300/315 = 1.52. Extra air mass = 1.52/1.33 = 1.14, about 14 percent more charge for the same boost.
chapters.trap: Intercooling does not raise the boost pressure; it raises the density at the same pressure. Saying the intercooler 'increases pressure' loses the mark.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.6 for pressure ratio, compressor heating and the turbine side.
chapters.leave: Cooler core design and nozzle vane aerodynamics are outside this unit; emission effects are in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A two-stroke must push out burnt gas and fill the cylinder in one short overlap, and the port layout decides how well it does that.
chapters.depth: Cover the need: no separate exhaust stroke, so a blower or crankcase pump supplies fresh charge. Define delivery ratio, scavenging efficiency and trapping efficiency, and show how they differ. Types: cross scavenging with transfer and exhaust ports opposite, loop or Schnuerle scavenging with the transfer streams meeting and forming a loop, and uniflow scavenging with inlet ports at one end and an exhaust valve or opposed piston at the other. Compare air used, mixing losses, short-circuiting and power per litre. Mention crankcase-scavenged small engines, reed and piston-port valves, and why uniflow gives the best scavenging but needs more hardware.

figure.aria: Tree of scavenging types with cross flow, loop scavenging and uniflow, each showing its main construction features.
figure.caption: Uniflow keeps the fresh charge moving in one direction, so it wastes the least air.

chapters.example: A two-stroke cylinder has a swept volume of 300 cm³. In one cycle the blower delivers 240 cm³ of fresh charge measured at outside conditions. Trapping efficiency is 0.80, so the fresh charge actually kept in the cylinder = 0.80 × 240 = 192 cm³. At exhaust port closure the cylinder holds 300 cm³ of mixture. Scavenging efficiency = 192/300 = 0.64, that is 64 percent. Delivery ratio = 240/300 = 0.80.
chapters.trap: Delivery ratio, trapping efficiency and scavenging efficiency are three different numbers. Delivered volume is not trapped volume, because part of the fresh charge leaves with the exhaust.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for two-stroke port timing; chapter 4.5 for why a blower is needed at all.
chapters.leave: Port timing diagrams and crankcase pumping detail to Unit 1; emission effects of short-circuiting to Unit 6.
